turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, doctor, thank you for fitting me in. I just... I don't even know the best way to explain it, really, because it's just so frustrating and it's been building up to the point where I just had to make an appointment. I came in because I feel like... well, I feel like I just cannot settle inside my own skin anymore. It's this awful, constant feeling. 

I'm 66 years old, I'm not working anymore, so my days are my own, and everyone tells me I should be relaxing and enjoying my time. Taking it easy. But I can't. I feel like I constantly have to jump up and do the next thing, whatever that is. I'll sit down in the living room, thinking I'll just rest my feet or look out the window for a minute, and before I even realize it, I'm back up again, looking for something to wipe down or put away or just moving around the house. 

And the absolute worst part is that I am just so worn out. My body is tired, you know? I should be sitting still. I really, really should be just sitting still and resting my bones, but my body just won't let me. It's like this motor that just won't turn off even when it's completely out of gas, and I just can't take living like this every single day.

symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient reports feeling 'so worn out,' having a tired body, and being 'completely out of gas.'

turns.doctor_question: When you feel this constant need to move around and can't sit still, do you also notice that your mind feels worried or anxious, or is it more of a physical sensation where your body just feels uncomfortable staying in one place?
turns.patient_response:
Well, that is a really interesting way you put it, because my daughter, she’s always asking me that same sort of thing. She’ll come over and see me pacing around the kitchen island wiping down the counters for the third time, and she’ll say, "Mom, what’s eating at you? Are you worried about something? Is it the grandkids?" And I always have to tell her, no, it’s really not like that at all. It’s not like I’m sitting there chewing my fingernails over the electric bill or fretting about the roof leaking—though heaven knows everything is so expensive lately, I just paid nearly five dollars for a dozen eggs at the market yesterday and I nearly dropped them right there in the checkout line. But no, it’s not a worry in my head like that. 

It’s just... well, it's exactly like you said, it's this physical thing. It’s like my body itself is just entirely uncomfortable. I’ll be sitting in my favorite armchair—it’s this lovely floral recliner I got at Macy’s maybe ten, twelve years ago, supposed to be the most comfortable chair in the world—and I’ll try to just watch Jeopardy. But my brain isn’t worrying about the trivia or anything else, my body is just... rebelling, I suppose you could call it. My legs get this sort of crawling feeling, and my arms feel like they need to stretch, and I just get this awful, tight feeling right under my skin if I stay put. It's like my bones are just itching to move. I just cannot stand the feeling of being planted in one spot. So I get up, and I wander into the hallway, and I’m not worried about the hallway, I just absolutely have to be on my feet to make that awful physical feeling stop.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes being unable to stay seated in her armchair while trying to watch TV, stating she has to get up and wander.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an intense physical sensation of restlessness, noting a crawling feeling in her legs and a tight feeling under her skin if she stays put.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient explicitly denies that her restlessness is driven by mental worry or anxiety, stating it is not a 'worry in my head'.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned your legs get a crawling feeling when you're sitting down. Does this crawling sensation in your legs happen mostly at night when you're trying to sleep, or does it happen throughout the day whenever you try to sit still?
turns.patient_response:
Well, see, that’s just the thing, doctor, it’s not just at night at all. I mean... yes, nighttime is awful, don't get me wrong, trying to lay in bed and get to sleep is a whole other ordeal, but it’s really all day long. It's any time I try to sit still, no matter what the clock says. 

Take yesterday morning, for example. I got up around 6:30, which is my usual time, and I made myself a nice cup of Folgers. I have this little breakfast nook in the kitchen—it gets the most beautiful morning light, my late husband put the window in for me years ago—and I thought, 'I'm just going to sit here, enjoy my coffee, and watch the birds at the feeder.' I have these lovely cardinals that come every single morning. But... well, I barely got two sips in, sitting right there on the cushion, and that crawling feeling started up in my legs. Just this absolute, overwhelming need to stand up. So I ended up drinking my coffee pacing around the kitchen island again. 

And then in the afternoon, it’s the exact same thing. If I try to sit on the back porch, or in the recliner, or anywhere... it doesn't matter if the sun is shining or if it's pitch black outside. If my bottom hits a chair, my legs start doing that crawling, restless thing within minutes. It’s so exhausting because there is just no safe time of day to take a load off. I just want to sit and read my Danielle Steel novels, I have a whole stack of them from the local library sitting right there on the end table, but I can't even get through a single chapter without my legs demanding that I get up and walk down the hall. So, no, it's definitely not just a nighttime problem, it's every single time I try to just... be still.

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly describes a 'restless thing' in her legs and an overwhelming need to stand up whenever she tries to sit.
symptom_reasoning.S027: The patient notes that 'trying to lay in bed and get to sleep is a whole other ordeal', indicating difficulty falling asleep (initial insomnia).
symptom_reasoning.S028: The patient reports observable psychomotor agitation, such as pacing around the kitchen island and walking down the hall because she cannot sit still.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any actual jerking or twitching movements in your legs when you get that crawling feeling, or is it purely a sensation without any visible movement?
turns.patient_response:
Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I was just talking to my neighbor Susan about this the other day. She’s the one who lives in the blue house next door, the one with the gorgeous hydrangea bushes that I am just so jealous of, I can never get mine to bloom like that. Anyway, we were standing out by the mailboxes, and she asked me something similar because her husband, Frank, he gets these terrible twitches in his legs when he sleeps. She says it’s like sleeping next to a bicycle pedaler, he just kicks and jerks all night long. 

But for me... no, I don't think it's like that. I haven't really noticed my legs actually jumping or jerking on their own, you know? It’s not like my knee just kicks out by itself like when they tap you with that little rubber hammer at the doctor's office. It’s... it's all on the inside. It’s that awful, awful feeling I was telling you about, that crawling, itching, tight sensation right under my skin. It’s so intense that it *makes* me want to move them. I'm the one doing the moving, if that makes sense. I have to physically stand up and walk or shake my leg out on purpose to make the feeling stop. But as far as them just twitching or jerking all by themselves without me telling them to? No, I really don't think I've ever seen them do that. It’s just that unbearable feeling that forces me out of my chair every single time.

turns.doctor_question: When you get up and walk around or move your legs, does that crawling, restless feeling in your legs go away, or does it stay the same even when you're moving?
turns.patient_response:
Well, let me think about that for a second... you know, it's really the only thing that gives me any peace at all. When I finally give in and just stand up—because I do try to fight it, doctor, I really do try to just sit there and be good and watch my program—but when I finally just heave myself up out of that chair and start walking, oh, it's like taking a deep breath after you've been holding it underwater. The crawling feeling just... it just goes away. It really does. 

Like yesterday, when I was telling you about my coffee at the breakfast nook? The second I stood up and started pacing around the island, wiping down the granite—I use that nice Meyer's cleaner, the lemon verbena scent, it just smells so fresh, my daughter got me hooked on it—anyway, the second I was up and moving, my legs felt perfectly fine. Completely normal! It's just a miracle, really, how fast it stops. But... and this is the really frustrating part, the part that just makes me want to pull my hair out... the minute I think, 'Okay, the feeling is gone, I can sit back down now,' and I go back to my cushion to finish my Folgers, it starts right back up again. Not even five minutes later! 

So, yes, the moving definitely makes it go away, completely away, but I have to *keep* moving, you see? I can't just walk to the kitchen and come back. I have to stay on my feet, walking, pacing, doing dishes, sweeping the floor—I swept the front porch three times on Tuesday just to keep my legs busy. So it works, but it's like a temporary fix. As long as I'm moving, I'm fine, but the second I stop... well, we're right back to square one with that awful, itchy, tight feeling under the skin. It's just exhausting, doctor, it really is, having to constantly be in motion just to feel comfortable in my own body.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned the crawling feeling happens all day long, but I want to make sure I understand the full picture: Is the sensation worse at certain times of day, like in the evening or at night, or is it pretty much the same intensity whether it's morning, afternoon, or nighttime?
turns.patient_response:
Well, you know, it's hard to say exactly if it's worse at one time or another because it just feels so awful whenever it happens. I mean, like I said, it happens in the morning when I try to have my coffee, and it happens in the afternoon if I try to sit and read my Danielle Steel. It just feels like this constant, nagging thing that’s always there waiting for me the second I try to sit down. 

I guess... I don't know, maybe I haven't really paid close enough attention to whether the feeling itself is actually stronger at night versus the morning. It’s just that at night, you know, you're *trying* to sleep, so you're stuck there in bed, and you can't just get up and start sweeping the porch like I do during the day. So maybe it feels more frustrating then? But the actual crawling sensation... the intensity of it... I really couldn't tell you if it's worse at 8 PM or 8 AM. It just feels equally terrible every time my bottom hits a cushion or a mattress. I wish I could give you a better answer, I really do, but it just feels like it’s always at an eleven on a scale of one to ten, no matter what time the clock says.

turns.doctor_question: When you're up and actively moving around during the day—like when you're doing your chores or walking through the house—do you ever feel that crawling, restless sensation in your legs even while you're already on your feet, or does it only happen when you're sitting down or lying still?
turns.patient_response:
Well, let me think about that... you know, when I'm actually up and moving, like really moving, I don't think I feel it. It's funny, because you'd think if something was wrong with your legs, it would hurt or bother you when you're using them, right? Like when my sister Margaret had that trouble with her knee—she had to have the whole thing replaced, bless her heart, and she was in physical therapy for months—hers hurt the most when she walked on it. But for me, it's the exact opposite! 

When I'm up, say, vacuuming the living room rug—and I have one of those heavy Dysons, my son bought it for me for Christmas two years ago because he said it was the best on the market, but honestly, it weighs a ton, I have to use both hands just to push it around the sofa—but when I'm doing that, pushing that heavy thing back and forth, my legs feel perfectly fine. Not a single tickle, no crawling, nothing. It's only when I finally turn the vacuum off, wrap the cord up—and I'm very particular about wrapping the cord neatly, I can't stand it when people just bunch it up—and I go to sit down on the sofa to catch my breath... that's when it starts. The second I'm still. 

So, no, if I'm already on my feet, if I'm walking to the mailbox or standing at the stove stirring a pot of soup—I made a lovely chicken noodle yesterday, from scratch, none of that canned nonsense—as long as I'm standing there, I'm okay. I don't feel the crawling at all when I'm actively doing something on my feet. It's just the sitting. The sitting and the lying down. That's the enemy right there. As long as I'm moving, I'm safe from it, if that makes sense.

turns.doctor_question: Does anyone in your family—your parents, siblings, or children—have a similar problem with restless legs or a constant need to move around that they've had to deal with?
turns.patient_response:
Well, let me think about that for a minute... you know, I really don't think so. I've been trying to rack my brain, because I know sometimes these things run in families, don't they? Like my mother's side, they all had terrible eyesight, just blind as bats by the time they were fifty, and my father's side had the bad hearts—my poor uncle Henry had his first heart attack at forty-two, if you can believe it. But this... this leg thing? No, I really don't think anyone else has ever complained about it. 

I mean, my sister Margaret, like I mentioned before with her knee replacement, she had trouble walking, but that was pain, you know? Bone on bone, the doctor said. It wasn't this awful, itchy, crawling feeling. And my brother Thomas, well, he was always a bit of a fidgeter when we were kids, couldn't sit still in church to save his life, my mother used to pinch his arm black and blue just to keep him quiet in the pew. But he grew out of that years ago. He's a retired accountant now, sits in his La-Z-Boy all day watching golf, perfectly content. Never says a word about his legs bothering him. 

And my children... well, my daughter Sarah is always running around, but she has three boys under the age of ten, so of course she's exhausted and always on her feet! But she's never mentioned anything about her legs feeling restless when she actually does get a moment to sit down. And my son David, he works in one of those big office buildings downtown, sits at a computer for eight, nine hours a day. If he had this, he'd be going out of his mind, wouldn't he? He'd never be able to keep that job. So, no, as far as I know, I'm the only lucky one in the family who has to deal with this... this absolute torture every time I try to just sit and enjoy a cup of coffee or watch my programs. It's just me.
